GraceChangeDesignContext.Rationale: Count at the door, identify no one. The 2026-10-28 research session established that the honest way to answer the standing question (owner, 2026-10-28, translated: "how many clicked Update") is server-side counting on our own domain: Tauri's official endpoint placeholders carry the client's version on every check, and distinct URLs for updater artifacts separate button clicks from site downloads by construction — the same file downloaded from two different links is two different counters, no client changes needed. A redirect-only worker is the smallest possible gateway: it adds one hop, stores one aggregate datapoint, and cannot corrupt the feed because it never produces a body; every redirect target is derived from validated inputs, so the gateway is not an open redirector. The fallback endpoints entry keeps today's GitHub behavior one non-2XX away, so the change cannot break updates when the gateway is slow, wrong or gone. Trust is untouched: artifacts verify against the app-pinned minisignature exactly as before — URL indirection is not trust (the argument the C-UPDATER-ROLLBACK restore already relies on). Privacy posture is preserved by construction: no IP, no user agent, no identifiers, day-level aggregates only — consistent with the site's «no analytics» promise made about the app; the privacy page is amended so every network-activity statement on it stays true — a false "no servers" line would be worse than no counting at all. Analytics Engine's free tier (100k writes/day vs an expected tens) and its three-month retention are accepted as-is: a rolling window is enough to steer releases; a warehouse is not being built. The owner's request of 2026-10-29 ordered the spec+plan passes with the full review protocol (owner, 2026-10-29, translated from Russian: "with the four-corner review and two clean passes").

Alternatives.Alternative: In-app telemetry (opt-in ping on update click): rejected — the app has zero analytics by design, its CSP forbids renderer egress, and any client ping is both a privacy regression and useless for the shipped fleet (old clients never report).

Keep reading GitHub asset counters only: rejected — no check visibility, no history, no Windows split (site and updater share the exe), and scanner noise (the research measured 39 tar.gz against 16 feed fetches: the counters cannot be a funnel).
Proxy the manifest through the worker (fetch GitHub and return the body): rejected — a proxy bug could poison the feed for every client; a 302 keeps the bytes GitHub's.

Count restore traffic too (route the C-UPDATER-ROLLBACK fetches through the gateway): rejected — restore is recovery, not funnel analytics, and its two-fetch contract is pinned by an applied change's tests.
A visible dashboard: rejected for v1 — the owner-run query script answers the standing question; UI can come later if the habit sticks.

DeferredDecisions.Decision: The exact worker route pattern and account binding names in wrangler.toml — fixed at implementation from the owner's zone layout (updates.mark.xronocode.com assumed; the plan re-confirms the zone exists before writing wrangler.toml).
Whether the query script speaks Analytics Engine SQL over GraphQL or the REST export — chosen at implementation; both are owner-token one-liners and the output shape is pinned either way.
The privacy-page sentence wording (mark-site, EN) — drafted at implementation; the spec pins its content (aggregate daily counts, version and OS only, no identifiers), not its prose.

Scenarios.Scenario: The standing question answered: after the first release with the new manifest, the owner runs query.mjs and reads — on 2.9.1's second day: 120 checks (day × os), 41 pkg darwin fetches, 6 pkg windows fetches (Update clicks, exactly measured — while plain downloads stay the derived GitHub-side approximation: asset total minus pkg, read from the GitHub counters), and the day 2.9.2 ships, from=2.9.1 appears in checks — the update-success number, measured without a single line of client telemetry.
Gateway outage: the worker 5xxes; the updater's endpoints array falls through to GitHub on the non-2XX; the check succeeds exactly as today; the only casualty is that day's numbers.
A scanner hits /pkg/windows-x86_64/../../evil — the gateway 404s with no datapoint and no redirect; nothing about the gateway reflects input into a Location header.

C-1.Name: Gateway outage or 5xx
C-1.Situation: The worker is down, rate-limited or erroring during a client's periodic update check.
C-1.Expected: The updater treats the non-2XX as a miss for that entry and continues to the second endpoints entry — the GitHub latest.json — so the check completes exactly as before; auto-checks and manual checks both keep working; the only effect is that the outage window is absent from the counters (undercounting, never breakage).

C-2.Name: Gateway never speaks for the feed
C-2.Situation: Any bug, compromise or misconfiguration of the worker that could affect manifest content.
C-2.Expected: A correct or misconfigured worker cannot affect content: every route is redirect-only — a Location header and no body it made — so the manifest bytes a client parses always come from the redirect target. A COMPROMISED worker controls the Location header and can point anywhere; the honest bound is what can be applied, not where it can point: the pinned minisign key lets only project-signed artifacts install (never arbitrary code), the updater's default version check additionally refuses downgrades, and any anomaly surfaces as from-transition outliers in the counters.

C-3.Name: Not an open redirector
C-3.Situation: Malformed or hostile input: /pkg/../../evil, /pkg/unknown/1.0.0, /feed with garbage parameters, unexpected paths, scanner traffic.
C-3.Expected: Strict validation (platform against the two-entry table, version against strict semver) means every unrecognized input gets a plain 404 with zero datapoints and zero redirects; every Location header ever produced is one of the derived GitHub URLs; nothing from the request appears in any response target.

C-4.Name: Mixed fleet rollout
C-4.Situation: Old clients (pre-config-change) and new clients coexist after the change ships.
C-4.Expected: Old clients keep checking GitHub directly (uncounted) but read whatever latest.json the newest release publishes — so their artifact fetches count at the gateway as soon as the first R-3 manifest ships; new clients' checks count too (R-2 config); coverage grows monotonically with releases and is reported honestly (the README and query tool state which population each number covers).

C-5.Name: Windows split finally exists
C-5.Situation: A Windows user clicks Update in-app; another downloads the installer from the website.
C-5.Expected: The in-app click resolves through /pkg/windows-x86_64/{ver} (counted as a pkg event) while the website link stays the direct GitHub asset (uncounted by us) — the two populations separate by URL construction, replacing today's single mixed counter; the minisignature against the app-pinned key verifies the installer identically on both paths.

C-6.Name: Counting write fails
C-6.Situation: The Analytics Engine binding is absent, throttled, or errors on a request.
C-6.Expected: The response is identical to the healthy case — the datapoint write happens inside waitUntil, its failure is swallowed with a log line, and the redirect still returns; counting is best-effort by contract, and no client ever waits on or notices the datastore.

C-7.Name: Retention window
C-7.Situation: The owner queries numbers older than three months, or wants year-over-year history.
C-7.Expected: The query tool and README state the Analytics Engine three-month retention plainly; day buckets are UTC; queries outside the window return nothing rather than inventing data; long-term storage is a recorded NonGoal (a future export change if the rolling window proves too short) — no data-loss claims are made beyond the window.

C-8.Name: Update success attribution
C-8.Situation: The owner asks how many of the clickers actually landed on the new version.
C-8.Expected: No client code exists for this and none is added: a success is the appearance of from={new version} among later checks (the placeholder carries it); the query tool prints the from-breakdown and the README explains the reading and its honest limits (a user who updates and never launches again is invisible; a fresh site install of N also reports from=N — the pkg and site counters separate the populations).

C-9.Name: Privacy posture unchanged
C-9.Situation: Any user or reviewer asks what Mark now tracks.
C-9.Expected: The app still contains zero analytics and its CSP still forbids renderer egress (pinned by a source scan); the gateway records day-level aggregates (event, OS/platform, version) with no IP, no user agent, no identifiers; the site privacy page says exactly this in the amended disclosure; no cross-session or cross-user correlation is possible from the stored data by construction.

C-10.Name: App Store edition
C-10.Expected: Nothing: the mas overlay strips the updater block entirely, store builds never touch the gateway, and their update story stays the store's own; the privacy-page sentence scopes itself to the download edition.

C-11.Name: Rollback paths untouched
C-11.Situation: A user runs the C-UPDATER-ROLLBACK restore while the gateway is in place.
C-11.Expected: The restore behaves exactly as its applied spec pinned: two direct deterministic GitHub fetches, offline on macOS; the gateway neither counts nor intermediates restore traffic, and a gateway outage cannot affect a rollback (recovery never depends on analytics infrastructure).

C-12.Name: Release pipeline discipline
C-12.Situation: The R-3 edit lands in release.yml while releases remain owner-gated.
C-12.Expected: The feed composition changes in code and CI (the build lane stays green; the manifest shape is pinned by the static fragment tests, and the first live proof is the owner-gated release), and no release runs, tags or publishes follow from merging this change; the first real release that carries the new manifest is a separate owner authorization, and until then the feed is byte-identical to today's.

Review.Findings: Round 6, consolidation pass by a fresh agent. VERDICT: clean — zero blocking, zero important, zero notes. Together with round 5 this completes the two-consecutive-clean-passes gate over all four corners (six rounds total; the decisive catch was round 4's {{target}} OS-name substitution finding, which silently would have killed all check counting). The spec is approval-ready.

Round 5, consolidation pass by a fresh agent. VERDICT: clean (0 blocking, 0 important, 2 advisory notes). First clean pass of the required two consecutive. Notes applied between passes: the success-reading honest-limits list gains the fresh-install caveat (a new site install of N also reports from=N; the pkg/site counters separate the populations); the AE quota citation re-anchored to the operative Workers free-plan request cap (100k requests/day; each gateway request writes at most one datapoint) with the three-month retention kept from the AE limits page.

Round 4, consolidation pass by a fresh agent. Verdict: changes-requested — 1 blocking, 1 important, 1 note. (F1 BLOCKING) the /feed os validation named the platform table {darwin-aarch64, windows-x86_64}, but {{target}} substitutes the bare OS name (darwin/windows — v2 docs and plugin source); validating the wrong table would have 404'd every legitimate check silently (updates alive via the fallback, counting dead) — /feed now validates its own OS table {darwin, windows} in R-1 and the criterion, the /pkg platform table unchanged. (F2) tests/renderer/release-preflight.test.js pins the exact single-element endpoints array — added to AffectedAreas with the two-entry expectation. (F3) the last untranslated owner phrase in the Rationale translated with speaker and date.

Round 3, consolidation pass over all four corners by a fresh agent (the two-agent dispatch hit a provider usage limit; the single-agent consolidation follows the C-UPDATER-ROLLBACK plan-gate precedent). Verdict: changes-requested — 0 blocking, 2 important, 4 notes; round-2 propagation verified complete (no unpropagated fix found). (F1) Assumption 2 mis-cited the hosting record — restated to the truth: the zone is DNS-managed in Cloudflare (C-22 DNS-only CNAME), the site is served by GitHub Pages (C-64 D-1), and the Worker route is zone-level configuration. (F2) R-8 named an impossible bump site — tauri.conf.json is strict JSON with no in-file markers; the in-file bump list now names release.yml only and the config edit's record is the change bundle. Notes also applied: the README pin gains the downloads-vs-clicks reading; the two Russian owner quotes in the Rationale translated in place; the ReviewLog location named correctly; the NonGoal reworded to state only exclusions.

Round 2, two fresh independent agents. Verdict: changes-requested — 1 blocking, 4 important, 7 notes; all fixed in the same edit pass. The round-1 fixes had not propagated to every surface (the recurring failure mode of this gate): (F1 BLOCKING) Summary and the Client-config criterion still demanded the arch placeholder R-1/R-2 had dropped — unified to exactly two placeholders; (F2) C-2 claimed absolutes under the "compromise" premise it itself postulated — reworded to the honest bound (a compromised worker can point anywhere; only project-signed artifacts apply, downgrades additionally refused by the default version check); (F3) the privacy page's opening "no analytics, no telemetry" framing added to the R-6 reconciliation set; (A4/F6) AffectedAreas still said "one sentence" — reworded to the full R-6 amendment. Notes also applied: non-GET methods in the 404 criterion; os/from validation and exact case-sensitive matching pinned in R-1; days-are-UTC in the normative README pin; download-edition scoping in the R-6 disclosure; the xronicode→xronocode typo; the active-bundle list corrected (C-TITLEBAR-MODE-CHIPS archived meanwhile — verified against the directory); doubled-word and dating nits.
